A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.
